facts.statement: Stemec fossils are found in the Late Oligocene Sooke Formation of British Columbia.
facts.quote: The genus is known from terrains dated from the Late Oligocene Sooke Formation of British Columbia

facts.statement: The first remains of plotopterids from the Sooke Formation were discovered in 2013 near Sooke by Leah and Graham Suntok.
facts.quote: the first remains of plotopterids from the formation were only discovered in 2013 in the vicinity of Sooke by Leah and Graham Suntok.

facts.statement: Gary Kaiser, Junya Watanabe, and Marji Johns described the new species Stemec suntokum in 2015.
facts.quote: In 2015, those remains were described by Gary Kaiser, Junya Watanabe and Marji Johns as the new genus and species Stemec suntokum

facts.statement: The genus name Stemec comes from the Coast Salish language, meaning an indefinite long-necked black waterbird native to the discovery area.
facts.quote: The genus name, Stemec, designate an indefinite long-necked black waterbird in the Coast Salish language native of the area in which the holotype was discovered.

facts.statement: The species name suntokum honors the family name of the discoverers, Leah and Graham Suntok.
facts.quote: The type species name, suntokum, honours the family name of Leah and Graham Suntok, the discoverers of the holotype.

facts.statement: Stemec was a relatively small plotopterid, similar in size to its Miocene relative Plotopterum.
facts.quote: Stemec was a relatively small plotopterid, comparable in size with its Miocene relative Plotopterum.

facts.statement: The holotype coracoid measures 74.8 mm in length and 12.8 mm in width, though erosion has damaged part of its surface.
facts.quote: The holotype coracoid is 74.8 mm long, 12.8 mm wide, and fairly complete, although erosion had damaged part of its surface.

facts.statement: Fossils found in coastal deposits suggest that the smallest plotopterids like Stemec had coastal habits, unlike larger, older relatives that were pelagic feeders.
facts.quote: The discovery of Stemec and its close relative Plotopterum in coastal deposits indicate that the latest and smallest plotopterids had costal habits, when the larger and older tonsalin plotopterids where pelagic feeders.

facts.statement: Stemec's osteology suggests it was not a proficient swimmer like larger relatives, which may explain why smaller plotopterids survived while larger ones did not.
facts.quote: Elements of their osteology indicates that they were not proficient swimmer like their larger, open sea specialist relatives, which may explain both the apparent lack of competition between larger and smaller plotopterids and the later survival of the latter form.

facts.statement: Stemec lived between 27.3 and 23.04 million years ago during the Chattian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Chattian to Chattian (27.3 to 23.04 million years ago)
